text: David Sweet, born on June 24, 1957, was a former Canadian Member of Parliament who served from 2006 to 2021. He initially represented the riding of Ancaster—Dundas—Flamborough—Westdale from 2006 to 2015, and after the 2012 federal electoral district redistribution, represented Flamborough—Glanbrook from 2015 to 2021. A member of the Conservative Party, he served as Shadow Minister for International Rights and Religious Freedom from 2019 to 2020. Throughout his parliamentary career, Sweet held various committee roles, including chair and vice chair positions. During the 42nd Canadian Parliament, he served as chair of the Conservative Party's parliamentary national caucus. Sweet was born and raised in Kingston, Ontario, to Gordon, a former Canadian Armed Forces sergeant and television repairman, and Jean Sweet, with five siblings. At age 13, he ran away from home and lived on the street for several months before being caught and sent to St. Joseph's Training School in Alfred, Ontario, a province-run institution for "incorrigible" youth. There, he endured physical beatings by Catholic brothers and bullying from other boys, with guards failing to intervene. He attempted to escape and was placed in solitary confinement for ten days; at one point, he was forced to scrub walls with bleach using his bare hands for three hours. He remained at the school until age 16. Before entering politics, Sweet owned and operated a variety of businesses, including a tow truck business in Mississauga from 1978 to the early 1980s, a real estate brokerage during the 1980s building boom, and a management consulting firm for 17 years, which provided training services to corporate, public, and not-for-profit clients. In 1996, he founded the Canadian Association of Professional Speakers. In 2004, he contested the Conservative Party nomination in Ancaster—Dundas—Flamborough—Westdale, defeating incumbent John Bryden, and placed second to Russ Powers in the 38th federal election. In advance of the 39th federal election, he secured the Conservative nomination again and won the seat on January 23, 2006, defeating Russ Powers. Upon arriving in Ottawa, he was appointed to and later elected vice-chair of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Public Accounts, and became a member of the Veterans Affairs Committee and the Subcommittee on International Human Rights. On June 22, 2006, he secured unanimous consent for a motion awarding honorary Canadian citizenship to the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, the third person to receive such an honour after Raoul Wallenberg in 1985 and Nelson Mandela in 2001. He won re-election in 2008, defeating Arlene MacFarlane-VanderBeek by over 10,000 votes. During the 40th Parliament, he served on the Veterans Affairs Committee, Liaison Committee, and International Human Rights Subcommittee, and was named Chair of the Industry, Science and Technology Committee in the third session, a role he maintained. On February 17, 2009, he was elected Chair of the Veterans’ Affairs Committee, a position he held since 2006, and also served as vice-chair of the Public Accounts Committee. On February 10, 2011, he introduced Private Member's Bill C-620, which aimed to amend the Corrections and Conditional Release Act to include victim impact statements in parole reviews; the bill was debated once on March 23, 2011, before the 40th Parliament dissolved. In the 2011 election, he won re-election in Ancaster—Dundas—Flamborough—Westdale, receiving more than double the votes of Liberal candidate Dave Braden. During the 41st Parliament, he remained Chair of the Industry, Science and Technology Committee and a member of the Liaison Committee and International Human Rights Subcommittee. On February 27, 2013, he introduced Private Member's Bill C-479, which aimed to strengthen victims' voices in the parole process and allow the Parole Board of Canada to extend parole review intervals for violent offenders; the bill passed through both the House of Commons and Senate, received all party support, and was given Royal Assent on April 23, 2015. Following the 2012 redistribution, the riding of Ancaster—Dundas—Flamborough—Westdale was split into Hamilton West—Ancaster—Dundas and Flamborough—Glanbrook. In the 42nd Canadian election, Sweet won re-election in Flamborough—Glanbrook, defeating Jennifer Stebbing. On November 5, 2015, he became the first elected Chair of the National Conservative Parliamentary Caucus, a role previously appointed by the party leader; in this capacity, he organized and chaired Conservative Caucus meetings. During the 42nd Parliament, he served as Vice Chair of the Subcommittee on International Human Rights and briefly participated in the Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage during a study on Motion 103. He was re-elected in Flamborough—Glanbrook in the 2019 federal election, again defeating Stebbing. On November 29, 2019, he was named Shadow Minister for International Human Rights and Religious Freedoms by then-leader Andrew Scheer. On October 8, 2020, he was elected Chair of the Standing Committee on Access to Information, Privacy, and Ethics. In January 2021, Sweet was found to have traveled to the United States during the COVID-19 pandemic, despite the border being closed to nonessential travel and public health advisories; the trip had been approved by Conservative Party leader Erin O'Toole, initially for a property issue and also for leisure. He resigned from the ethics committee and announced he would not seek re-election. Sweet has frequently spoken about mental health, particularly following the death of his daughter Lara in 2017. In a Member's statement, he urged the Government of Canada to adequately fund the Canadian Mental Health Commission and support the Canadian Mental Health Association. In 2019, he supported Private Members' Motion 174, which sought a National Strategy on Suicide Prevention, and in his speech shared the day Lara died by suicide, emphasizing that four thousand people take their lives annually in Canada, often among youth or family members, and that a national strategy could unite organizations working on mental health and suicide prevention. During the 2019 federal election, Sweet campaigned on his advocacy for mental health, committing to increased funding for mental health research and programs and promoting the National Strategy on Suicide Prevention. Though not a federal jurisdiction, Sweet has repeatedly called on the Ontario government to launch a public inquiry into so-called "training schools" like the one he attended as a child. In a letter to then Attorney General Yasir Naqvi, he criticized the lack of recognition and support for victims of only three of sixteen such institutions, noting that all thirteen unacknowledged institutions were run by the provincial government, and argued that an inquiry would provide recommendations to prevent future injustices, inform the public about what happened to children, and demonstrate the government's commitment to justice. Naqvi declined the request. Sweet is a vocal critic of Iran, describing it as a state that "terror, supports terrorist groups like Hamas and Hezbollah, imprisons, tortures and executes its own people and others," and has presented multiple petitions urging Canada to maintain Iran's designation as a state supporter of terrorism and oppose any rollback of sanctions. He has highlighted the persecution of Baháʼí followers in Iran, calling for the release of the Baháʼí Seven—Fariba Kamalabadi, Jamaloddin Khanjani, Mahvash Sabet, Afif Naeimi, Saeid Rezaei, Vahid Tizfahm, and Behrouz Tavakkoli, whom he says were "wrongfully imprisoned." A staunch supporter of Israel, Sweet has traveled to Israel multiple times, including with Prime Minister Stephen Harper and Governor General David Johnston. He has repeatedly condemned antisemitism and anti-Israel sentiments in the House of Commons, denouncing the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement as "nothing but thinly veiled antisemitism, and to be very frank, Jew hatred," and has criticized Israel Apartheid Week as a "concerted effort to demonize and delegitimize the right of the State of Israel to exist and the Jewish people to have a safe homeland therein." He has also served as both chair and vice chair of the Canada-Israel Interparliamentary Group. Sweet is a strong advocate for human rights and religious freedoms, having served on the House of Commons Subcommittee on International Human Rights since 2006, which has studied issues such as the Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar, child slavery, the persecution of Uyghur Muslims in China, religious minorities in Pakistan, and the protection of women human rights defenders. He served on the Steering Committee of the Canadian Parliamentary Committee to Combat Antisemitism (CPCCA) and on the CPCCA's Inquiry Panel, which released a public report on July 7, 2011. In November 2012, he received the 2012 Humanitarian Award from the Hamilton Jewish Federation for his work with CPCCA and his anti-racism advocacy. Sweet makes an annual Members Statement in June to recognize Scleroderma Month in Canada, noting on June 1, 2006, that his mother died from complications of scleroderma and cancer. He also attends annual Scleroderma walks in Hamilton and across Ontario to advocate for research into a cure. He lives in Ancaster, Ontario, with his wife Almut, and they have five children—Chris, Lucian, Reuben, David Jr., and Lara—and four grandchildren. He also has a daughter, Theresa, from a previous marriage. In 2017, Lara, whom David and Almut adopted, died from an intentional drug overdose. On September 19, 2017, Sweet delivered a Member's statement in her memory, stating that she reshaped his thinking on whether someone has to be "all together" to assist others. Sweet is a motorcycle enthusiast and has spoken in the House of Commons on road safety for motorcyclists. He participates in charity motorcycle rides across Ontario, including Hamilton's Liberty for Youth Eagle Ride. In April 2014, he was inducted as a Knight in the Order of St. George.
